A.title: Austria Gambling Reform Reaches Final Committee Stage
A.excerpt: Austria's Gambling Act overhaul went before the Finance Committee on 24 November. What the 31 December exit deadline means for operators.
body: Austria's long-awaited liberalisation of online gambling has reached its final parliamentary stages. The Federal Act amending the Gambling Act and the Telecommunications Act 2021 was listed as the main item before the National Council's Finance Committee (Finanzausschuss) on Tuesday 24 November 2026. According to reports of the parliamentary schedule, once the committee has completed its review, Finance Committee Chairman Andreas Ottenschläger is to sign the bill off so that it can be scheduled for a plenary vote in the National Council. The committee itself cannot make amendments that would require a fresh decision of the full chamber, so the text that emerges is expected to be substantially the text operators will have to work with.

The reform would end the exclusive position held for decades by Österreichische Lotterien and replace it with a multi-concession model. Under the government's timetable, a licensing window would open on 1 January 2027 and the regulated online market would launch on 1 October 2027. For international groups that have treated Austria as a grey market, served from Malta or other EU licences and defended by reference to EU free-movement arguments, this is the most significant change in the Austrian market since the current Gambling Act was enacted.

The provision that will demand immediate attention is the transitional condition reported in the draft timetable: operators currently serving Austrian customers without a domestic licence must withdraw by 31 December 2026 if they wish to qualify for a concession. That leaves barely five weeks. A credible exit is more than a geoblock. Operators should expect to have to show that registrations from Austria are closed, existing accounts have been dealt with and balances returned, marketing and affiliate activity aimed at Austria has stopped, and payment flows have ended, with documentary evidence of each step. Regulators in other liberalising markets, including Germany and the Netherlands, have treated conduct during the cooling-off period as central to suitability, and Austria is likely to do the same.

The exit decision also interacts with litigation risk. Austrian courts have for years been the leading European forum for player claims seeking repayment of losses from operators without an Austrian licence. Leaving the market does not extinguish claims relating to past play, and a concession applicant will need to explain how historic exposure is being managed. Groups should review whether their exit communications to customers could be used as admissions, and coordinate the regulatory and litigation strategies rather than running them separately.

Timing is complicated by Brussels. The draft was notified under the EU's technical regulations procedure (TRIS). The standstill period was originally due to end on 5 November, but the Commission's register now shows 7 December after Malta delivered a detailed opinion, and the Commission has also submitted comments. A detailed opinion extends the standstill and requires Austria to explain how it will respond. Under settled CJEU case law, a technical regulation adopted in breach of the standstill obligation can be unenforceable against individuals, so the date of final adoption matters. Malta's intervention is also a reminder that Maltese-licensed operators, and the Maltese state, see Austria's transition rules as a test of how far a member state can condition market access on past conduct.

The bill also gives the authorities new tools. Reports indicate it would introduce a central exclusion register, deposit limits that apply across operators, tighter rules for online slots and land-based gaming machines, and powers to block websites and payments. According to the parliamentary briefing as reported, the exclusion register and the website and payment blocking measures are to enter into force on 1 January 2027, the day after the withdrawal deadline. Operators that remain in the market into January should expect enforcement activity to begin quickly, with payment service providers and ISPs receiving the first orders.

What should operators do now? First, decide whether Austria is a market worth applying for once concession numbers, fees and tax terms are known, and do not wait for those details before starting an exit plan. Second, prepare application materials in parallel: corporate structure and beneficial ownership, AML and player protection frameworks, and technical integration for the central register and cross-operator limits. Third, review supplier and affiliate contracts so that Austrian-facing activity can be shut down cleanly by 31 December. Austrian and Maltese gaming counsel can help operators model the timeline against the TRIS outcome and the final text adopted by the National Council.

A.title: KSA Blocks Betsson Shirts in Champions League Matches
A.excerpt: The Dutch regulator stopped Inter and Club Brugge showing Betsson, or its foundation, in Dutch fixtures. What it means for sponsorship deals.
body: The Netherlands Gambling Authority (Kansspelautoriteit, KSA) has shown that its sponsorship rules reach visiting clubs in European competition. Working with the Dutch football association (KNVB), the KSA prevented Inter Milan and Club Brugge from displaying Betsson branding on their shirts during UEFA Champions League matches in the Netherlands: Inter's game at Feyenoord on 3 November 2026 and Club Brugge's match against PSV Eindhoven on 4 November. Betsson is the front-of-shirt sponsor of both clubs and does not hold a Dutch licence.

The clubs proposed a compromise: wearing Betsson Foundation branding in place of the commercial brand. The KSA refused. In its published statement, the regulator said the foundation's name and styling were not sufficiently distinguishable from the unlicensed operator, so displaying it would still promote illegal gambling. Inter played without a front-of-shirt sponsor, and Club Brugge carried the slogan of its own charitable foundation. No fine or formal sanction has been reported against either club.

The legal basis is the Dutch ban on sponsorship by online gambling operators, which took full effect in 2025 and, according to reports, prevents even licensed operators from placing their messaging on shirts. In this case there was a second, independent problem: promoting an operator without a Dutch licence is itself prohibited under the Betting and Gaming Act. The KSA says it contacted foreign clubs and associations before the season to explain that the ban applies to them, and it has asserted exclusive authority over gambling messaging on shirts in the Netherlands, including at international competitions.

The rejection of the foundation branding is the most important legal point. Regulators across Europe are increasingly alert to surrogate advertising, where a charitable arm, a free-to-play product or a media brand shares the name, colours or typography of a gambling operator. The KSA's approach is functional: it asks whether the average viewer would associate the message with the gambling brand, not whether the entity named is legally separate. Operators that rely on look-alike brands to keep visibility in restricted markets should assume that test will be applied to them.

The case also raises a question of territorial reach. The KSA's action concerned what players wore on the pitch in the Netherlands, not how the clubs present themselves at home or how broadcasts appear in other countries. Dutch viewers will still see Betsson-branded shirts in away fixtures broadcast from Italy or Belgium. The regulator has nonetheless made clear that it will act where it can: in its own territory, through the national association and the match organisers. Belgium, home of Club Brugge, is itself phasing out gambling sponsorship of professional sport, so the exposure for Belgian clubs will only increase.

The same KSA update also reported action on product scope. The regulator ordered Circus and ZEbet to remove markets on the NBA Coach of the Year award and the AFL Brownlow Medal, because Dutch licensees may only offer bets on sporting competitions and awards decided by a jury or panel are excluded. Both operators complied, said no customers had placed bets, and attributed the markets to human error. Taken together, the two actions show a regulator applying its rules strictly on both sides: what licensees offer and who is allowed to be seen.

For clubs, sponsors and agencies, the lesson is contractual. Sponsorship agreements with gambling brands should include territory-specific carve-outs, an agreed alternative kit for restricted markets, and clear allocation of the cost of lost exposure. Sponsors should not assume that a foundation or secondary brand will be accepted as a substitute. UEFA competition fixtures should be checked against host-country rules before each round. Dutch gaming counsel can advise on how the KSA applies its advertising and sponsorship rules, and how they interact with the regimes in Belgium, Italy and Sweden.

A.title: MGM Exits NCPG Over Prediction Market Funding
A.excerpt: MGM Resorts and BetMGM have cancelled their NCPG memberships over a $2m prediction market grant. The compliance stakes for RG programmes.
body: The dispute over prediction markets has reached the responsible gambling sector. MGM Resorts International and BetMGM have rescinded their memberships of the National Council on Problem Gambling (NCPG), as first reported by the Las Vegas Review-Journal. The move follows NCPG's acceptance, about six months ago, of a $2 million grant from the prediction market industry, and its creation of a Financial Services and Trading membership category that allows prediction market companies to join.

The letter to NCPG was signed by Stephen Martino, Senior Vice President and Chief Compliance Officer of MGM Resorts, and Rhea Loney, Chief Compliance Officer of BetMGM. It argues that no organisation should understand the risks of prediction markets better than NCPG. NCPG responded that the departures send a political message and do nothing to prevent gambling-related harm. Its board president, Derek Longmeier, said NCPG is neutral on whether prediction markets should be legal but not neutral on harm prevention, and that it regards prediction markets as functionally gambling.

MGM is not alone. According to reporting, the Michigan Gaming Control Board, the Ohio Casino Control Commission and the Nevada Council on Problem Gambling have also withdrawn their affiliations, and NCPG's executive director resigned in September. The $2 million grant is funding NCPG's Financial Trader Health and Safety Initiative, for which it is now recruiting a senior manager. The fact that state regulators have stepped back makes this more than a disagreement between trade bodies.

The compliance stakes are real. State-licensed operators work within detailed responsible gaming requirements: helpline messaging, self-exclusion integration, staff training, limit-setting tools and, in many states, annual responsible gaming plans submitted to the regulator. Prediction market platforms regulated by the CFTC are not subject to those state rules. Licensed operators' central objection is that a body funded by unlicensed competitors may become less willing to argue for parity of player protection. Whether or not that concern is borne out, it creates governance questions about the independence of a key industry partner.

There is an irony that litigators will notice. NCPG's statement that prediction markets are functionally gambling supports the position taken by the states in the event contract litigation with Kalshi and others. Courts have split on whether sports event contracts listed on CFTC-designated contract markets pre-empt state gaming law, and characterisation is central to that debate. A respected harm-prevention body describing the products as gambling is not legally decisive, but it is the kind of evidence that may be cited in briefs and in regulators' public statements.

For operators, the practical step is to review responsible gambling partnerships. Compliance teams should identify where their programmes depend on external bodies for training content, certification, helpline services, research or conference participation, and check whether any regulatory submissions refer to those relationships. If an operator withdraws from a body, it should be ready to show the regulator that the functions provided through that relationship are still covered. Funding relationships should be reviewed for conflicts of interest and disclosed where state rules or internal policies require.

Prediction market companies face the mirror image. Funding harm-prevention work is a sensible way to show responsibility, but it now carries reputational risk and may be presented by opponents as an attempt to buy legitimacy. Platforms should ensure that grants are structured with clear independence protections and that their own player protection tools are robust on their merits. US gaming counsel can advise on how state responsible gaming obligations apply to operators' partnerships, and on how the prediction market debate is likely to develop in the 2027 legislative sessions.

A.title: PAGCOR Sanctions Operators Over Lucky Spin Jackpot
A.excerpt: PAGCOR found no manipulation in the Lucky Spin jackpot dispute but still sanctioned operators for breaching approved game manuals.
body: The Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR) has sanctioned licensed online gaming operators following public complaints about the Lucky Spin jackpot feature. Players had circulated screenshots of what appeared to be jackpot wins, but said they never received the pop-up notification that should confirm a jackpot. PAGCOR announced the outcome of its review on 24 November 2026.

PAGCOR's findings were in two parts. On integrity, the regulator found no evidence of manipulation, tampering or irregularities. System records matched the game results, and according to PAGCOR none of the complainants had in fact won the jackpot. On compliance, it nonetheless found that the operators had breached their approved manuals and applicable regulations, and it accepted that the way the game operated had caused public confusion. PAGCOR did not name the operators or disclose the penalties.

The separation of those two findings is the key point for operators everywhere. A regulator does not need to find that a game was rigged to impose sanctions. Licensed games are approved on the basis of specific documentation: rules, paytables, display logic and player notifications. Any deviation between the approved manual and what players actually see is a regulatory breach in its own right, even if the random outcomes are fair. Where the deviation produces confusing displays, such as screens that look like a win when no win has occurred, the regulator is likely to treat it as a consumer protection issue as well.

The screenshots also show how quickly player disputes become public. Social media evidence of an apparent win, combined with an operator's refusal to pay, leads to reputational damage well before any regulatory review concludes. Operators should have an escalation process that treats a cluster of similar complaints as a potential system issue, not as a series of individual disputes, and that preserves game logs and client-side data immediately so the operator can show what actually happened.

Similar principles apply in other major regulated markets. The UK Gambling Commission's remote technical standards require game information and outcomes to be displayed accurately and not to mislead, and the Malta Gaming Authority requires changes to approved games to go through formal change control. In each case the burden is on the licensee, not the supplier, even where the game was developed by a third party. PAGCOR's decision reflects the same approach: the licensed operators were sanctioned for the way the feature was presented to players.

The decision comes as the Philippine online gaming sector is under heavy political and regulatory scrutiny, with debate continuing over restrictions on online gaming and advertising. In that environment, operators should expect PAGCOR to act on visible player-facing problems quickly and publicly, even when the underlying technical issue turns out to be limited.

Practical steps follow. Operators should audit live games against their approved manuals, paying particular attention to win animations, jackpot notifications and promotional overlays added after certification. Change management should ensure that front-end changes, including those made by suppliers, are assessed for whether regulatory approval is needed. Supplier contracts should allocate responsibility for compliance failures and include cooperation duties for regulatory investigations. Gaming counsel with Asian and European experience can help operators align game approval processes across markets.

A.title: Ghana Gaming Commission: 2027 Budget Sets AML Focus
A.excerpt: Ghana's 2027 budget reports 58 illegal operations shut and 88 licences issued in 2026, with AML/CFT and digital regulation next.
body: Ghana's 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy, presented to Parliament on 12 November 2026 by Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, gives a detailed account of the Gaming Commission of Ghana's work over the past year and sets out its priorities for 2027. For operators looking at West Africa, the figures show a regulator that is licensing actively while increasing enforcement, and that intends to focus next on anti-money laundering and digital supervision.

On licensing, the Commission issued licences to 88 operators and granted 14 promotional permits in 2026. On enforcement, it shut down 58 illegal gaming operations, closed six illegal casinos and confiscated 1,350 banned analogue slot machines. It completed 79 of 81 investigations, carried out 272 inspections and 144 surveillance operations, and imposed 25 sanctions. It also opened four zonal offices, in Agona Swedru, Asante Bekwai, Ho and Sefwi Wiawso, extending its presence beyond Accra.

Player protection figures are also included. The Commission processed 4,607 self-exclusion requests and ran awareness programmes for 9,324 students. Self-exclusion on that scale implies operators need working processes to receive and act on exclusion notices from the regulator. International entrants should check how their platforms will handle national exclusion lists and whether local requirements differ from those in their home markets.

The Commission's non-tax revenue was GH¢96.673 million for January to September 2026, with a full-year projection of GH¢120.656 million and a 2027 projection of GH¢130.464 million, an increase of about 8%. The wider budget introduces no new taxes and leaves corporate tax at 25%. That gives some stability after the recent changes to betting taxation, including the abolition in 2025 of the 10% tax on winnings, although operators should still model corporate tax, VAT and levy exposure carefully.

The Commission's stated priorities for 2027 are oversight, responsible gaming, compliance and enforcement, AML and counter-terrorist financing controls, digital regulation and institutional capacity. The AML focus is significant. Gaming operators are accountable institutions under Ghana's Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2020 (Act 1044), and international pressure on AML frameworks in the region means supervisors are paying more attention to customer due diligence, source-of-funds checks and suspicious transaction reporting. Operators should expect more on-site inspections and data requests focused on AML in 2027.

Digital regulation is the other theme to watch. Ghana's legal framework, the Gaming Act, 2006 (Act 721), was drafted before mobile betting became the dominant channel, and the Commission's reference to digital regulation suggests further technical requirements for online and mobile operators. These could include server location, real-time reporting, payment integration with mobile money providers, and stronger action against offshore sites accepting Ghanaian players.

For international groups, Ghana remains one of the more developed regulated markets in West Africa, but entry now requires investment in local compliance infrastructure. Applicants should plan for local incorporation and ownership structures, AML programmes that meet local reporting requirements, integration with national self-exclusion processes, and careful tax structuring. African gaming counsel can advise on licensing strategy in Ghana and how it compares with Nigeria, Kenya and South Africa.
